title: Establish that an exoplanet hosts life

concept.text: The innovation would be a convincing astronomical demonstration that a planet orbiting another star hosts life. Observations would reveal several mutually reinforcing signs of biological activity, interpreted alongside the planet’s atmosphere, environment and host star. Detecting a gas that life could produce would begin this investigation; establishing that biology best explains the combined evidence would be the decisive advance.

The central challenge is interpreting remote evidence. Atmospheric chemistry can reflect biological and nonbiological processes, and its meaning depends on planetary conditions and stellar history. The concept therefore combines astronomy, planetary science, atmospheric chemistry and astrobiology: observations and models must jointly establish why the measured signals indicate an inhabited world.

significance.text: Conditional significance: confirmation would establish a second known location hosting life, extending the empirical study of living worlds beyond Earth. It would provide an actual extraterrestrial case against which ideas about habitable environments and detectable biological effects could be assessed. This is a reasoned consequence of the proposed discovery, rather than an achievement reported in the supplied evidence.

The initial comparisons with Earth would be limited to the information observations could recover. Atmospheric measurements could support comparisons of environmental conditions and possible biological effects on planetary chemistry. Detailed comparative biology would require additional capabilities and evidence; establishing an inhabited atmosphere would not itself reveal organisms, their molecular machinery or their evolutionary history.

Conditional limits: one confirmed inhabited exoplanet would not establish how frequently life arises, how widespread it is across different planetary environments, or whether the terrestrial and extraterrestrial biospheres originated independently. Those questions would require further observations and, for independent origins, evidence capable of distinguishing separate origins from a shared biological history.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability is to move from atmospheric characterization and candidate biosignatures to a robust inference of life. A single potential biosignature is insufficient because a measured chemical feature can admit nonbiological explanations. The breakthrough would require enough independent information to test biological and abiotic models against the same planetary evidence.

The scientific barriers include constraining atmospheric chemistry, planetary interiors and environmental conditions, together with the effects of the host star and its evolution. These factors determine whether a proposed biological product could instead arise or persist without life. Follow-up observations and extensive atmospheric modeling must narrow the alternatives sufficiently for the biological interpretation to remain convincing.

Engineering synthesis: the observations must also be reliable enough that instrumental effects, data processing choices or contamination associated with the star cannot plausibly account for the apparent planetary signal. Geological explanations and observational artifacts are reasonable parts of this assessment, although the supplied review notes that the NASA article does not separately analyze them. Obtaining repeatable measurements and enough contextual information to distinguish competing explanations remains part of the proposed capability.

current_state.text: NASA’s April 18, 2025 discussion describes Webb’s demonstrated ability to characterize exoplanet atmospheres. Its infrared observations allow scientists to investigate atmospheric chemical composition and obtain clues about habitability and potential biosignatures. These achievements supply part of the observational foundation for a future life-detection case; the article reports no confirmed detection of exoplanet life.

The same discussion explains that a potential biosignature alone would not establish life. Confirmation would require follow-up studies, multiple converging lines of evidence and assessment of false positives, potentially drawing on independent observations from multiple missions and extensive atmospheric modeling. Webb’s observations are described as helping build the scientific and technical foundation for future missions, rather than completing that confirmation process.

Evidence boundary: the supplied material supports this dated account, but it does not establish a field-wide status through November 1, 2026. The review reports an empty freshness-search record. A September 2026 page-update footer does not demonstrate that the April 2025 article comprehensively reassessed intervening life-detection claims. Consequently, neither a later confirmation nor the continued absence of one can be resolved from these inputs.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: independent observations of the same exoplanet would establish several mutually reinforcing signs of biology, supported by sufficient atmospheric, planetary and stellar context to evaluate credible abiotic explanations. The measurements and contextual models would need to support a coherent biological interpretation across the combined evidence. This proposal follows NASA’s discussion of converging evidence and false-positive assessment; it is not an established universal certification standard.
completion_criteria.label: Converging biosignatures and planetary context support a coherent biological interpretation

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility criteria: the essential signals should survive repeat observations and independent analyses, with agreement across instruments or missions where feasible. The case should make measurement uncertainties, model assumptions and remaining alternative explanations explicit, so other researchers can assess whether the conclusion depends on a particular observing setup or analysis choice. No numerical threshold for confirmation is established by the supplied material.
completion_criteria.label: Essential signals survive repeat observations and independent analyses

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical boundary: excluding credible abiotic explanations would mean testing physically plausible alternatives within the available observations and modeling limits. It would not mean proving that every conceivable nonbiological explanation is impossible. Evidence specifically indicating ongoing biological activity would strengthen the case, but this is an additional proposed condition, not a requirement attributed to NASA. Finite observations would establish the breadth of conditions and alternatives actually tested, without guaranteeing that every possible explanation had been exhausted.
completion_criteria.label: Credible abiotic alternatives tested within observational and modeling limits

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: AST-02, “Detect an independently verifiable extraterrestrial technology,” overlaps with this concept in its need for independent verification and careful exclusion of alternative explanations. The target evidence differs: AST-01 concerns life, which could be microbial and produce no technology; AST-02 concerns technological activity. A technological discovery securely associated with an exoplanet could contribute to a life case, but the two entries retain distinct objectives and evidentiary routes.

Roster-based synthesis: AST-08, “Produce resolved surface maps of rocky exoplanets,” could supply spatial information useful for interpreting a planet’s environment and possible biosignatures. A resolved map would not by itself establish life, and AST-01 does not necessarily require a resolved surface map if atmospheric and contextual evidence proved sufficiently convincing. The concepts therefore overlap in planetary characterization while defining different achievements.

Roster-based synthesis: the remaining entries address separate astronomical targets: dark matter and cosmic acceleration in AST-03 and AST-04; primordial and millihertz gravitational waves in AST-05 and AST-10; early cosmic structure, the first stars and early massive black holes in AST-06, AST-11 and AST-13; gravity near black holes in AST-07; neutrino observations in AST-09 and AST-12; and coronal heating in AST-14. They share broad practices of inference and verification with AST-01, but the supplied roster establishes no direct dependency or equivalence with exoplanet life detection.

change_log.change: Preserved AST-01 and its original title while expanding the explanation around converging astronomical evidence.
change_log.reason: The candidate, research and review consistently identify the advance as establishing an inhabited exoplanet, beyond detecting a possible biosignature.

change_log.change: Replaced the undated claim that no potential biosignature has established life with an April 18, 2025 source-bounded account and an explicit freshness limitation.
change_log.reason: The article reports no confirmed detection, but the empty freshness record cannot establish the state of the entire field through November 1, 2026.

change_log.change: Qualified comparative biology by the information remote observations could recover and retained the limits concerning prevalence and independent origins.
change_log.reason: An inhabited-world detection would establish another location hosting life without automatically revealing detailed biology or resolving its origin.

change_log.change: Integrated planetary interiors, atmospheric chemistry, environmental conditions and stellar evolution into the explanation of the missing capability.
change_log.reason: The review identifies these contextual factors as essential to assessing biological and nonbiological interpretations.

change_log.change: Distinguished proposed geological and observational-artifact checks from the source’s directly discussed contextual framework.
change_log.reason: The review considers these reasonable components but notes that the article does not separately analyze them.

change_log.change: Framed completion criteria as proposals, bounded exclusion of abiotic alternatives by observational and modeling limits, and made ongoing activity a strengthening condition.
change_log.reason: The supplied evidence supports the general approach without establishing a universal standard or requiring proof against every conceivable alternative.

change_log.change: Used the article-level source without repeating the candidate’s section locators.
change_log.reason: The review reports that the named sections are absent from the retained article and that the relevant passages occur in its unheaded body.

change_log.change: Added explicit relationships to AST-02 and AST-08 and a bounded distinction from the remaining roster.
change_log.reason: This preserves the separate concepts while explaining their relevant overlap without inventing dependencies.

unresolved_issues: The supplied evidence does not resolve whether exoplanet life had been established by November 1, 2026, or by the later source-retrieval date.
No particular exoplanet, combination of biosignatures, numerical confidence threshold or observing program is specified; the completion criteria remain a general proposal.
The supplied source does not separately substantiate detailed geological false-positive mechanisms or observational-artifact controls.
The extent of biological information recoverable from a future confirmed detection, and whether it could establish independent origins, remains unknown.

brief.title: Convincing evidence of life on another star’s planet
possible: We could know that Earth has company as a living world. Astronomers would connect several signs of biological activity on a planet orbiting another star, using its atmosphere, environment and star to establish that life best explains what they see.
why: A second known living world would give scientists an extraterrestrial case to compare with Earth. They could test ideas about environments that support life and how living things change a planet’s chemistry.

sources.showed: NASA describes Webb’s ability to study the atmospheres of small planets around cooler stars. It explains why confirming life would require several lines of evidence and tests of explanations that do not involve life.
sources.quote: While not designed to search for life on other planets, Webb’s performance has made it the first observatory capable of characterizing the atmospheres of some of the most promising small planets orbiting cooler stars.
sources.cited_for: Webb provides atmospheric measurements that could contribute to a future case for life.
sources.not_established: Measuring atmospheric gases does not establish that biology produced them.

sources.showed: In a preprint, the team reported tentative signs of dimethyl sulfide (DMS) or dimethyl disulfide (DMDS), sulfur-containing gases that life might produce, on K2-18 b.
sources.quote:
The spectrum shows distinct features and is inconsistent with a
featureless spectrum at 3.4-σ significance compared to our canonical model.
sources.cited_for: The observations prompted a specific claim of possible gases associated with life.
sources.not_established: The gas identities remain uncertain, and the observations do not establish a biological source.

sources.showed: The team’s preprint found insufficient evidence for DMS or DMDS when it combined Webb observations. Other molecules fit equally well, and the result depended on processing and modeling choices.
sources.quote:
We find that any marginal preferences are the
result of limiting the number of molecules considered in the model and oversensitivity to small changes between data reductions.
sources.cited_for: The proposed gas detections did not hold up across different analyses and competing molecular explanations.
sources.not_established: This analysis does not determine whether the planet hosts life.

sources.who: Sean Jordan, Shang-Min Tsai, Paul B. Rimmer and Oliver Shorttle
sources.showed: Their preprint modeled a route that could produce detectable DMS and DMDS without life. Its effectiveness depends on an experimentally unmeasured barrier to a chemical reaction.
sources.quote:
We
demonstrate that one proposed formation pathway is capable of producing observable abundances of
abiotic DMS and DMDS, however it depends sensitively on the energy barrier of the limiting step, which
remains unmeasured experimentally.
sources.cited_for: Chemistry without life could complicate the interpretation of these sulfur-containing gases.
sources.not_established: The model does not establish how much of these gases this route actually produces on K2-18 b.

sources.showed: Their models found that planets around small, cool stars could lose water and accumulate oxygen without life. A star’s early history can therefore affect how atmospheric oxygen should be interpreted.
sources.quote:
We ﬁnd that the amount of water lost scales with
the planet mass, since the diﬀusion-limited hydrogen escape ﬂux is proportional to the planet surface
gravity.
sources.cited_for: Oxygen can have a nonbiological origin, making planetary and stellar history essential context.
sources.not_established: These models do not establish the history or biological status of a particular observed planet.

shown: NASA’s Webb telescope can measure atmospheric chemistry on some small planets around cooler stars. This gives astronomers a way to investigate possible signs of life from afar.
Madhusudhan’s team reported tentative sulfur-containing gases on K2-18 b. Luque’s team found that the combined observations did not robustly establish those gases. The claim remains disputed.
missing: Several independent signs of life must fit the same planet’s atmospheric and environmental conditions.
The essential signals must survive repeat observations and independent analyses, with instrumental and stellar effects accounted for.
Observations and models must test credible chemical and geological explanations that do not involve life.

milestones.label: Several signs support life in the planet’s known conditions
milestones.explanation: Independent observations would have to reveal mutually reinforcing signs of life, supported by knowledge of the planet and star. Together, they would make a coherent biological explanation possible.

milestones.label: Essential signals survive repeated observations and independent analysis
milestones.explanation: The essential signals would have to persist across repeat observations and independent analyses, with agreement across instruments where feasible. This would reduce dependence on a particular setup or analysis choice.

milestones.label: Credible explanations without life withstand explicit testing
milestones.explanation: Physically plausible explanations without life would have to be tested within observational and modeling limits. This would establish how thoroughly alternatives had been challenged without claiming to exclude every possibility.

uncertain: How strong the combined evidence must be to count as confirmation remains an open question.
How much biology atmospheric observations could reveal, including whether life arose independently of Earth’s, remains unknown.

page.title: Detection of life on an exoplanet
page.definition: Astronomical observations establish biological activity on a planet orbiting another star. Biosignatures—observable effects that life can produce—fit the planet’s environment, withstand tests of nonbiological explanations and receive independent observational confirmation.

goal.need: Earth is the only known inhabited planet. Its atmospheric oxygen is one example of how life can change a world. On a distant planet, different gases can leave similar features in a spectrum. Confirming life on one exoplanet would establish that another planetary system is inhabited and give us a second world for comparison. Estimating how common detectable signs of life are takes a survey of comparable planets with known sensitivity to those signs. Even zero detections in such a survey can set an upper limit on their frequency.

statements.quote: HWO is the first observatory designed specifically to search for signs of life on exoplanets.

statements.body: National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, Astro2020 survey committee
statements.quote: to search for biosignatures from a robust number of about ~25 habitable zone planets
statements.context: The passage states an objective of the recommended infrared, optical and ultraviolet space observatory.

statements.quote: The ultimate goal of NASA's Exoplanet Program is to find unmistakable signs of current life.

completion.title: Independent observations confirm predicted biological behaviour on an exoplanet.
completion.criterion: For one exoplanet, reach level 7 of the proposed Confidence of Life Detection (CoLD) scale: independent follow-up observations confirm biological behaviour predicted for the environment, after the level 6 tests. The follow-up investigation is planned after the level 6 results. The framework does not prescribe a numerical probability or statistical-significance cutoff.
completion.set_by: Green et al. (2021), proposed Confidence of Life Detection scale, Figure 1 and discussion of level 7.
completion.threshold_quote: Independent, follow-up observations of predicted biological behaviour in the environment
completion.basis: CoLD connects its final stage with confirmation and explicitly discusses exoplanet applications. NASA’s guidance of 18 April 2025 likewise requires converging evidence and observations testing biological and nonbiological predictions. NASA describes CoLD as a proof-of-concept communication framework. These are published proposed criteria, not an adopted certification standard.

milestones.title: An exoplanet observation detects a signal of a kind that life is known to produce.
milestones.criterion: At CoLD level 1, detect a feature in observations of the exoplanet and identify it as a kind of signal known to arise from biological activity. Its source on that planet can remain unresolved.
milestones.set_by: NASA Astrobiology Program, proposed CoLD level 1, reproduced on slide 8 of Scalice (2025).

milestones.title: Terrestrial contamination is excluded as the source of an exoplanet’s candidate biosignature.
milestones.criterion: At CoLD level 2, rule out terrestrial contamination as the source of the candidate signal. For a space telescope, one source to exclude is light from Earth reflected off part of the spacecraft into the instrument.
milestones.set_by: NASA Astrobiology Program, proposed CoLD level 2, reproduced on slide 8 of Scalice (2025).

milestones.title: Biology can produce the detected signal under the exoplanet’s environmental conditions.
milestones.criterion: At CoLD level 3, demonstrate or predict that biology can produce the detected signal under the physical and chemical conditions of the environment where it was observed.
milestones.set_by: NASA Astrobiology Program, proposed CoLD level 3, reproduced on slide 8 of Scalice (2025).

milestones.title: All known nonbiological sources of an exoplanet’s candidate biosignature are shown implausible.
milestones.criterion: At CoLD level 4, show that every known nonbiological source of the detected signal is implausible under the conditions on the exoplanet.
milestones.set_by: NASA Astrobiology Program, proposed CoLD level 4, reproduced on slide 8 of Scalice (2025).

milestones.title: An additional independent candidate biosignature is detected on the same exoplanet.
milestones.criterion: At CoLD level 5, detect an additional signal on the same exoplanet that independently supports the biological interpretation. A surface pigment detected through its effect on reflected light could supply such evidence alongside an atmospheric biosignature.
milestones.set_by: NASA Astrobiology Program, proposed CoLD level 5, reproduced on slide 8 of Scalice (2025).

milestones.title: Follow-up observations rule out alternatives raised after an exoplanet biosignature announcement.
milestones.criterion: At CoLD level 6, use subsequent observations of the exoplanet to rule out alternative explanations for the candidate biosignature proposed after the original announcement.
milestones.set_by: NASA Astrobiology Program, proposed CoLD level 6, reproduced on slide 8 of Scalice (2025).

milestones.title: Remote observations of Earth recover a planetary signature of its biosphere.
milestones.criterion: Observe Earth remotely as a known inhabited planet and identify an atmospheric or surface feature attributable to its biosphere. This control tests whether a biological effect can be recognized in planetary observations.
milestones.set_by: The Earth control used by Sagan et al. (1993) and described in the National Academies’ Exoplanet Science Strategy (2018).
milestones.threshold_quote: observations of modern Earth as an exoplanet can be used to search for global impacts due to life.

not_found: No adopted numerical threshold for confirming exoplanet life was found in NASA guidance, Astro2020 or the biosignature-assessment frameworks searched.
No statement disputing the value or feasibility of the goal itself was found in the NASA and National Academies documents examined.

results.finding: One JWST MIRI transit of K2-18 b yielded 2.9–3.2σ evidence for DMS and/or DMDS.
results.detail: DMS and DMDS have overlapping absorption features in the MIRI band. The reported significance applies to evidence for at least one of the two gases.
results.quote:
We report new independent evidence for DMS
and/or DMDS in the atmosphere at 3-σ significance, with high abundance (≳10 ppmv) of at least
one of the two molecules.

results.finding: One K2-18 b transit implied ≥10 ppmv of DMS and/or DMDS, an abundance the authors argued cometary impacts could not supply.
results.detail: The photochemistry argument draws on short lifetimes in experiments, a nondetection of H₂S, and previously reported high CO₂. The paper calls for further tests of abiotic production in dry, methane-rich, reducing atmospheres.
results.quote:
In summary, cometary impacts can-
not be responsible for the relatively large DMS and/or
DMDS abundance inferred from the present MIRI re-
trievals.

results.finding: In one K2-18 b MIRI transit, CH₄ and CO₂ at their previously measured mixing ratios of about 1% each could not explain the features.
results.detail: The new spectrum bypasses the original cross-detector offsets by using MIRI. It leaves DMS and DMDS spectrally degenerate.
results.quote:
The contributions from
both molecules at previously measured abundances of
∼1% each are insufficient to explain the observed spec-
tral features in the present spectral range with JWST
MIRI (6-12µm).

results.finding: K2-18 b, 3 JWST transits: the largest reported Δ ln Z favoring DMS/DMDS was 2.8.
results.detail: Small differences between reductions near 7 and 10 µm changed which molecule was favored. The paper uses Δ ln Z ≥ 5 as its threshold for strong evidence.
results.quote:
In
no case does the preference for DMS /DMDS reach ∆ ln Z > 5,
considered standard for any molecule detection claim.

results.finding: K2-18 b, 3 JWST transits: the ethane model had Δ ln Z = +0.97 versus the DMS/DMDS model in the JExoRES retrieval.
results.detail: The difference is calculated from Table C.1 and falls within the paper’s statistically indistinguishable range. Ethane’s line list is incomplete.
results.quote:
We find that other generic hydrocarbons can provide an al-
ternative explanation for the putative DMS/DMDS spectral fea-
tures proposed by M23 and M25, as demonstrated with the
case of ethane (C 2H6) in this work.

results.finding: On K2-18b (one exoplanet), modeled abiotic DMS and DMDS together can reach the tentative retrieval’s lower bound at ≳10 ppm deep H₂S.
results.detail: Neither gas reaches the reported constraint on its own. The combined result depends on an unmeasured activation barrier and estimated upper limits for the final reaction rates.
results.quote:
Under the retrieval constraints for the atmosphere of K2-18b 7, abiotic production of DMS and DMDS by pathway
B can satisfy the tentative reported detections from N. Madhusudhan et al. (2025) within the lower bound of the 1σ
error threshold, if the deep H 2S abundance is≳10 ppm (Figure 3, left).

results.finding: For one modeled exoplanet, GJ 667Cc, runaway water loss could leave about 2,000 bars of abiotic atmospheric O₂.
results.detail: The estimate assumes a mass of five Earth masses and that the oxygen remains in the atmosphere. Whether it persists after the runaway depends on how efficiently surface sinks remove it.
results.quote:
In particular, this could be the case for GJ 667Cc,
which could have lost as many as 10 TO early on, accu-
mulating close to 2000 bars of O2; as a result, it may not
be habitable today.

results.finding: K2-18 b, one planet: the assessed upper limit for known abiotic DMS production under similar atmospheric conditions was 0.05 ppmv.
results.detail: The benchmark comes from laboratory photochemistry. The authors also weigh cometary delivery and interstellar abundances. The deep-atmosphere pathway remains open because the atmospheric structure and hydrogen sulfide abundance are uncertain.

results.finding: Across eight Earth earthshine spectra from one day, the vegetation red-edge slope correlated with cloud-free vegetated area at 0.91.
results.detail: The red edge was weak. Attribution depended on contemporaneous land and cloud distributions, with radiative-transfer modeling used to test whether changing cloud cover explained the observed variation.
results.quote:
We calculated the correlation between the decline
of normalized cloud-free areas of vegetation and the red-edge
decline for models and observations over the course of the ob-
servations.

results.detail: The primary retrieval used JexoPipe data, one instrument offset and no stellar heterogeneity. The authors interpret the methane abundance as consistent with chemical recycling in a deep hydrogen-rich atmosphere.

results.finding: JWST detected methane at up to 5.0σ across two transits of one exoplanet, K2-18 b.
results.detail: The methane detection is robust to the modeled instrument offsets. The separate dimethyl sulfide signal is marginal and sensitive to those offsets.
results.quote:
Among the prominent CNO molecules, we ﬁnd the strongest
detection for CH 4 at 4.7 σ–5.0σ across all three cases.

results.finding: HD 102195b, 144 spectra: water and methane were detected jointly at 5.3 σ after telluric correction.
results.detail: The 5.3 σ value compares cross-correlations along and away from the planet’s velocity track. It does not quantify the exclusion of all terrestrial contamination.
results.quote:
The two molecules are detected with a combined signiﬁcance of 5.3 σ, at a semi-amplitude of the planet radial veloc-
ity KP = 128± 6 km s−1.

results.finding: For one exoplanet, K2-18b, the inhabited Hycean model sustained 2% methane with an imposed biological flux.
results.detail: The imposed methane flux was about half Earth's modern biological flux. The model used a 30% reduction in incoming starlight to obtain a temperate surface. An abiotic mini-Neptune model fit the JWST data equally well.
results.quote:
Model 2 ﬁts the
CH4 and CO2 spectral features in the data because it has 2% of
biologically produced methane along with 0.8% CO 2.

results.finding: TOI-270 d, one JWST/MIRI transit: adding isoprene to a reduced atmospheric model yielded ln B up to 2.64.
results.detail: The highest isoprene value came from the cloud-free JexoPipe retrieval. Evidence was weak in the canonical retrievals, and several other molecules could explain the mid-infrared features.
results.quote: Notably, some of the best-fitting species identified include benzonitrile, methylacrylonitrile, isobutene, and potentially isoprene.

goal.need = "Earth is the only known inhabited planet. Its atmospheric oxygen is one example of how life can change a world. On a distant planet, different gases can leave similar features in a spectrum. Confirming life on one exoplanet would establish that another planetary system is inhabited and give us a second world for comparison. Estimating how common detectable signs of life are takes a survey of comparable planets with known sensitivity to those signs. Even zero detections in such a survey can set an upper limit on their frequency.". Reason: The survey target belongs with the programme statements, while the scientific rationale needs to explain what one detection could establish and what requires a survey.

add statement by NASA Exoplanet Program, 2026: "The ultimate goal of NASA's Exoplanet Program is to find unmistakable signs of current life.". Reason: The programme names an unambiguous detection of current life as its goal, beyond the existing statements about searching for candidate biosignatures.

Reason: The title can imply that the signal’s origin on the exoplanet is already known, and the criterion mixes the level 1 test with a disputed molecular identification.
